definition: Conative refers to tendencies of striving or impulse in mental life. In this source, it appears in the phrase “conative tendencies,” meaning action-oriented wants or urges more broadly than bodily appetite alone.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Appetite; pinned source text

reasons: “Striving” is not supported by the packet; the source only says “conative tendencies of all sorts” and recommends the terms “appetence” or “impulse” instead.
The gloss “action-oriented wants or urges” goes beyond the packet’s wording and adds an interpretive characterization not stated in the source.

The packet does not directly define “conative” as “tendencies of striving or impulse”; it only says that “Appetite” is “applied to conative tendencies of all sorts,” and that for these “appetence (or appetency) and impulse are better.”

The packet does not support the claim that the phrase “conative tendencies” in this source means “action-oriented wants or urges more broadly than bodily appetite alone.” The text contrasts “appetite” with “impulse” and discusses appetite as an organic need, but it does not spell out “action-oriented wants/urges” as the meaning of “conative.”
The definition adds broader interpretive wording (“impulse in mental life,” “more broadly than bodily appetite alone”) that is not explicitly supported by the provided excerpt.
